teaching.causalExplanation: The World Health Organization defines health promotion as the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health. Control is the key word. A hospital improves health. A campaign that tells people what to do, without changing their circumstances, adds information, not control. So health promotion isn't health care, which treats people who are already unwell, and it isn't just health education. It includes education, but also changes the conditions that decide whether education can be acted on. Australia has used three approaches, and each asks a different first question. The biomedical approach asks: what's wrong with this body, and how do we fix it? It's the narrow meaning you met at the start, health as no disease, turned into action. The behavioural approach asks: what's this person doing wrong, and how do we get them to stop? The socio-ecological approach asks: what conditions are producing this pattern, and who can change them? They aren't ranked. A broken leg needs the biomedical approach, and no amount of town planning will set it. All three still operate today, nested inside each other. The first shift, from biomedical to behavioural, came from a change in what was killing people. Early last century, infections dominated, and sanitation, vaccination and antibiotics beat them. By the nineteen seventies, the leading killers were heart disease and cancer, which develop over decades and are linked to smoking, diet, alcohol and inactivity. By the time they show up, much of the damage is done. So attention moved upstream, to behaviours.

It includes education, but also changes the conditions that decide whether education can be acted on.

scenes.teachingReason: Australia has used three approaches, and each asks a different first question. The biomedical approach asks: what's wrong with this body, and how do we fix it? It's the narrow meaning you met at the start, health as no disease, turned into action. The behavioural approach asks: what's this person doing wrong, and how do we get them to stop? The socio-ecological approach asks: what conditions are producing this pattern, and who can change them? They aren't ranked. A broken leg needs the biomedical approach, and no amount of town planning will set it. All three still operate today, nested inside each other.

scenes.teachingReason: Australia built on international agreements. The nineteen seventy-eight Declaration of Alma-Ata made primary health care the basis of Health for All. That's essential, affordable care close to home, including prevention, not just a GP visit. It also said health is made outside hospitals, across many sectors. The Ottawa Charter in nineteen eighty-six turned that into action areas, which is next time. Jakarta in nineteen ninety-seven added partnerships, including with business, and Bangkok in two thousand and five tackled globalisation and marketing. And UNESCO works with the WHO on health-promoting schools.
